newsitem.title: THAILAND: Cambodia forces agree to ceasefire in west.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia forces agree to ceasefire in west.

text.p: Cambodia's royalist forces have agreed to a ceasefire in the west with soldiers loyal to Second Prime Minister Hun Sen after failing to enlist the support of former Khmer Rouge guerrillas, rebel and Thai army sources said on Thursday.

The ceasefire was reached late on Wednesday after three hours of talks between the rival forces faced off at Bantea Meanchay, near Battambang, said a former Khmer Rouge commander now leading an independent army in the area.

Battambang, 250 km (150 miles) northwest of the capital Phnom Penh, is the second largest town in Cambodia. Skirmishes began there after Hun Sen's followers ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh from office in Phnom Penh on Sunday. Ranariddh was due to arrive in New York on Thursday.
Forces loyal to Ranariddh intend to make Battambang their base for a war of resistance against Hun Sen.

Sok Peab, commander of the Democratic National United Movement (DNUM) army comprising former Khmer Rouge guerrillas, said his group had refused a request from Ranariddh loyalists to help fight Hun Sen's advancing forces.
That decision, after the DNUM had been warned by Hun Sen forces not to get involved, forced the Ranariddh loyalists to agree to the ceasefire, he said.

"I was informed this morning that they had agreed to halt fighting at least for the time being," Sok Peab told Reuters by telephone from his base in west Cambodia. "We told both sides that the DNUM will not get involved in their feud."
The DNUM was formed last year by Ieng Sary after he broke away from the hardline Khmer Rouge of Pol Pot with some 4,000 followers.

Ieng Sary, 74, was foreign minister during Pol Pot's 1975-79 "killing fields" reign of terror during which more than a million Cambodians died through execution, torture, disease, starvation or overwork.
Thai army sources based in eastern Thailand's Aranyaprathet bordering Cambodia confirmed the reports of negotiations between the rival premiers' forces and said the situation was relatively calm.
"I think Ranariddh loyalist soldiers are not in a position to hold on for more than a couple days, so they sought to negotiate," an army source said.
A royalist officer who fled to Aranyaprathet from Cambodia told Reuters that Hun Sen had sent heavy reinforcements into the Battambang area from Phnom Penh, including 22 tanks into Battambang itself.
The officer said Ranariddh and Hun Sen forces shared control of Battambang, but royalists retained full control of nearby Sisophon, Bantea Meanchay and Poipet.

Cambodia's ambassador to the United Nations, a member of Ranariddh's royal family, told reporters in New York on Wednesday that the ousted prime minister planned to make Battambang his stronghold for a resistance war against Hun Sen.

"We will take Battambang, the second city. We have disarmed more than 2,000 (opposing) soldiers," the ambassador, Prince Sisowath Sirirath, told a news conference in his government's first detailed comments since Hun Sen's takeover of the capital.

An estimated 58 people were killed and almost 200 wounded in last weekend's fighting in Phnom Penh which has sparked condemnation from the United States and prompted neighbouring Southeast Asian countries and several Western nations to evacuate their citizens.
